1261.title: With the offering, to the offering
1261.hook: the Purusha Sukta's last verse: the world begins as an offering, and giving is the first dharma
1261.carry: yajna: the world began as an offering
1261.howItsDone: The Purusha Sukta is recited in Hindu worship and Vedic chanting. At home, many Hindus offer food to God before eating and receive it back as prasad, some saying Bhagavad Gita 4.24, brahmarpanam, before the meal.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, one body, and careful hands for a hard verse. Then the sky drawn from a body: the moon from his mind, the sun from his eye, the wind from his breath.
screen: `THE MOON, FROM HIS MIND.`

segments.voice: A jar on a kitchen counter, with a cloth over the top. Inside, a sour, bubbling paste: a sourdough starter. You make today's bread with a piece of yesterday's. You feed the starter, take some for the loaf, and keep the rest going for next time. Every loaf comes from the one before. Ask where the first starter came from, and the chain runs back further than anyone in the kitchen can see. The Purusha Sukta ends on a loop like that: its last two verses, and the first dharmas.
screen: `A JAR ON THE COUNTER.` → `TODAY'S BREAD FROM YESTERDAY'S.` → `A CHAIN RUNNING BACK.`

segments.voice: Verse fifteen gives the measurements of the great offering. Seven sticks were laid around its fire, and three times seven were made its fuel, when the gods, spreading out the offering, bound the Purusha as what was offered. Then verse sixteen, the hymn's last. Yajnena yajnam ayajanta devah. With the offering, the gods offered to the offering. It loops back on itself: the offering is the means, the one who receives, and the act, all at once. Then: tani dharmani prathamany asan. These were the first dharmas: the first right ways of things, set down by that offering. Here's the teaching, plainly. In this hymn the world doesn't start with a builder or a rulebook. It starts as yajna, an offering, and giving is the first dharma. Hindu life keeps that loop going at the table. The Bhagavad Gita picks it up: those who eat what remains of the offering are freed, it says, and those who cook only for themselves eat wrong. And many Hindus say a Gita verse before meals, brahmarpanam: the offering is Brahman, what's poured is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. Giver, gift and fire, all one, the same loop as the hymn's last line. That's why a plate goes before God first, and comes back as prasad. Many teachers read it as a way to live: nothing is simply taken. It's received, and passed on.
screen: `SEVEN STICKS, THREE TIMES SEVEN FUEL.` · `WITH THE OFFERING, TO THE OFFERING.` · `THESE WERE THE FIRST DHARMAS.` · `YAJNA: OFFER FIRST, THEN RECEIVE.`

segments.voice: Picture your next meal set in front of you, and don't start yet. Bring to mind where it came from: the soil, the rain, the hands that grew it, the one who cooked it. If you pray, offer it first, as many Hindus do, with the Gita's brahmarpanam or in your own words, then take it back as something given. If you don't pray, simply pause and say thank you before the first bite. When the real meal comes, do it for real.

1262.title: The king who became a seer
1262.hook: a king tried to seize a sage's wish-granting cow, lost everything, and became the seer of the Gayatri
1262.carry: the gayatri asks god to light the mind
1262.tomorrow: who is Savitr, the god the Gayatri calls?
1262.howItsDone: Hindus who keep the practice recite the Gayatri at dawn and dusk or with a mala, and many first name its seer, meter and god: Vishvamitra, gayatri, Savitr. In Vedic recitation it is learned as part of Rig Veda 3.62.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, you are a small copy of the cosmos, and a loop: with the offering, the gods offered to the offering, and these were the first dharmas.
screen: `A GIVING THAT FEEDS THE NEXT GIVING.`

segments.voice: A king rides through a forest with his whole army. A sage in a hermitage feeds every last soldier a feast, and the king asks how. A cow, the sage says: a cow that gives whatever is asked. The king decides he has to have her. He'll lose almost everything he tries next, and come out of it as one of the most honored seers in Hindu memory, the one tradition credits with the Gayatri. Today: the seer behind the verse.
screen: `A KING, AN ARMY, A HERMITAGE.` → `A COW THAT GIVES WHATEVER IS ASKED.` → `THE SEER BEHIND THE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Before many Hindus chant the Gayatri, they name three things: its seer, Vishvamitra; its meter, gayatri; its god, Savitr. In the Ramayana, Vishvamitra is born a king, not a priest. The sage is Vasishtha, and the cow is Shabala. The king offers thousands of cows for her, elephants, gold. Vasishtha says no. So the king takes her by force, and the cow fills the field with warriors who beat his army. He goes away, wins divine weapons through hard practice, and comes back. Every one of them falls into the sage's wooden staff and vanishes. And the king says, in paraphrase: a warrior's strength is nothing; a seer's strength is real. He walks away into tapas, years of hard practice. He stumbles, into anger, into desire, and begins again. At last Vasishtha himself greets him as a brahmarshi, a seer among seers. Tradition names him as the rishi who saw the Gayatri, and it sits in the Rig Veda's third book, the book of his family, partway through a hymn, the first verse to Savitr. Now listen to what it asks. Not for a cow, an army or a kingdom. Dhiyo yo nah prachodayat: may he stir our thoughts. Many teachers read the story and the verse together. The man who grabbed for a wish-granting cow is remembered for a prayer that asks only for light in the mind. That's the heart of the Gayatri: before anything else, ask God to help you see clearly.
screen: `SEER: VISHVAMITRA. METER: GAYATRI. GOD: SAVITR.` · `A WARRIOR'S STRENGTH IS NOTHING.` · `TAPAS, AND A SEER AMONG SEERS.` · `MAY HE STIR OUR THOUGHTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you want badly right now: a result, a yes, someone's approval. Hold it for a breath, then set it down beside you, like a king setting down his weapons. Now ask for one thing only, clear sight. If your tradition welcomes you to say the Sanskrit, say dhiyo yo nah prachodayat softly; if not, may our minds be lit is enough. Notice it says our, not my, and let the circle widen to the people around you.

1263.title: Savitr calls everyone home
1263.hook: a Vedic hymn sees Savitr at evening, calling everyone home. it's why the Gayatri is kept at dawn and dusk
1263.carry: sandhya: the gayatri at the day's two turnings
1263.tomorrow: why is the verse called the Gayatri at all?
1263.howItsDone: Hindus who keep sandhya recite the Gayatri at the day's turning points, dawn and dusk, so the verse to Savitr is said both as the day begins and as it closes.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gayatri asks god to light the mind: its seer, Vishvamitra, the king who learned to ask for light.

segments.voice: Six in the evening. A laptop lid clicks shut. Down the block, a shopkeeper rattles the shutter down. A bus fills with people heading home, and somewhere a pot goes on the stove. Nobody announced it, but the day has turned, and everyone stops at once. A Vedic poet watched this same hour and gave it a god, the god the Gayatri speaks to. Today: who Savitr is in the hymns.
screen: `A LAPTOP CLICKS SHUT.` → `EVERYONE STOPS AT ONCE.` → `THE POET GAVE THE HOUR A GOD.`

segments.voice: The Gayatri asks one thing of Savitr: may he stir our thoughts. To hear that fully, meet him in the other hymns. The Rig Veda pictures him in gold. One hymn calls him hiranyapani, golden-handed, coming on a shining chariot and looking over the creatures of the world. He's the sun, but more than the ball of light: the power that sets things going. A hymn in book two sees him at the other end of the day. When Savitr comes at evening, it says, in paraphrase, the weaver rolls up the cloth she was weaving. The worker sets down a task half done. The traveler turns toward home. The birds go back to their nests. Everything that was moving comes to rest, because Savitr has said so. So he isn't only the god of starting. He sends the world out, and he calls it home. That's why the Gayatri isn't only a morning prayer. Hindus who keep sandhya, the prayer of the joinings, say it where the day turns: at dawn, as Savitr sends everyone out, and at dusk, as he calls them back, and many at noon too. In plenty of homes, dusk is also when a lamp is lit. Asking this god to stir the mind isn't asking for endless motion. It's asking the one who knows when to begin and when to stop. The weaver doesn't finish her row. She rolls up the cloth because the hour has come, and the cloth will be there tomorrow.
screen: `THE GAYATRI SPEAKS TO SAVITR.` · `AT EVENING, THE WEAVER ROLLS UP HER CLOTH.` · `SANDHYA: PRAYER AT THE DAY'S JOININGS.` · `HE SENDS US OUT, AND CALLS US HOME.`

segments.voice: For the first half of the sit, let the breath be a little fuller, as if the day were starting. Halfway through, let it go back to its own pace and picture rolling up one piece of today's work, unfinished, and setting it aside. If you pray, keep sandhya tonight the way many Hindus do: at dusk, light a lamp if you can, and say the Gayatri or hold its meaning, may our thoughts be stirred. If you don't pray, still mark the hour: stop, roll up the work, and let the day close.

1264.title: The verse called a mother
1264.hook: a boy who couldn't name his father is taken in by a teacher: the thread ceremony as a second birth, with the Gayatri as mother
1264.carry: the gayatri gives a second birth
1264.tomorrow: why do we say Om bhur bhuvah svah first?
1264.howItsDone: At the upanayana, the sacred thread ceremony, a teacher or parent passes the Gayatri to the student, in many families whispered into the ear; students also learn it as an example of the gayatri meter, and older texts call it the Savitri.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhya: the Gayatri at the day's two turnings, kept at dawn and dusk for Savitr, who sends the day out and calls it home.
screen: `HE SENDS US OUT, AND CALLS US HOME.`

segments.voice: A boy named Satyakama wants to study the Vedas, and the teacher will ask about his family line. So he asks his mother, Jabala. She tells him the truth: she doesn't know who his father was; she was young and worked as a servant in many houses. Call yourself Satyakama Jabala, she says, my son. He walks to the teacher Gautama and repeats it word for word. The teacher says: no one but a true brahmin could speak like that. Bring firewood. I'll initiate you. Today: the verse at the heart of that initiation, and why an old law book calls it a mother.
screen: `A BOY WHO CAN'T NAME HIS FATHER.` → `HE TELLS THE TEACHER THE TRUTH.` → `BRING FIREWOOD. I'LL INITIATE YOU.`

segments.voice: That initiation is the upanayana, the sacred thread ceremony, and at its heart the teacher passes on one verse: the Gayatri, in many families whispered into the student's ear under a cloth. Older law books, like the Manusmriti, call that verse the Savitri, after Savitr, the god it speaks to. And the Manusmriti says something bigger. The ceremony is a second birth, and in that birth, it says, the Savitri is the mother and the teacher is the father. That's why one who has received it is called dvija, twice-born. Now hear Satyakama again. One way to read the two together: the boy who couldn't name a father is given one, his teacher, and a mother too, the verse. So why does almost everyone call it the Gayatri? Gayatri is the name of its meter. Vedic tradition counts three lines of eight syllables: tat savitur varenyam, bhargo devasya dhimahi, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat. Like a poem called a sonnet, it's named for its vessel; the hymn that opens the Rig Veda, to Agni, has the same shape. Traditions have differed on who receives it: the law books speak of boys, and today many families and movements teach it to daughters and to anyone who asks. Underneath sits the teaching: in Hindu life, receiving a sacred verse is a birth. You're born once to your parents, and again into a way of seeing.
screen: `UPANAYANA: THE SACRED THREAD.` · `A SECOND BIRTH: TWICE-BORN.` · `A FATHER, AND A MOTHER TOO.` · `GAYATRI: THE NAME OF A METER.` · `RECEIVING A VERSE IS A BIRTH.`

segments.voice: On each out-breath, count eight slowly in your head, one line of the meter; do it three times for three lines, then rest for a few natural breaths and begin again. If you lose count, start the line over. As you count, think of whoever first gave you a prayer, a verse or a way of seeing: a grandparent, a teacher, a parent. If you pray, give thanks for them; if you don't, simply hold them in mind.

1265.title: Earth, sky, heaven, then the verse
1265.hook: Om bhur bhuvah svah isn't in the Rig Veda's verse. it's the doorway: earth, the space between, the sky
1265.carry: stand in all three worlds, then pray
1265.tomorrow: what did a king ask a man who knew the Gayatri?
1265.howItsDone: In daily recitation, Hindus who chant the Gayatri may begin with Om and the three vyahritis, bhur bhuvah svah, before the verse itself; traditions vary on further additions.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri gives a second birth: named for its meter, called the Savitri, and in the thread ceremony, a mother.
screen: `A VERSE CALLED A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Open the Rig Veda to book three, hymn sixty-two, verse ten. Run a finger along the line, looking for the words that so often come first when the Gayatri is chanted: Om bhur bhuvah svah. They aren't there. The verse begins tat savitur varenyam. The opening sits outside it, like a doorway built in front of a house. Today: the words before the Gayatri, and why they're said.
screen: `BOOK THREE, HYMN SIXTY-TWO, VERSE TEN.` → `OM BHUR BHUVAH SVAH: NOT THERE.` → `A DOORWAY IN FRONT OF THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: In daily recitation the Gayatri is often framed. First comes Om, the sacred syllable. Then three short words: bhur, bhuvah, svah. They're called vyahritis, utterances. They aren't part of the Rig Veda verse; they come from the practice of reciting it, and from other Vedic texts that talk about them. One is the Taittiriya Upanishad. In paraphrase: bhur, bhuvah, suvar, these are the three utterances, and a teacher named Mahachamasya made known a fourth, mahas. Then it lays them out like a map. Bhur is this world, the earth. Bhuvah is the space in between. Suvar is the world beyond. And mahas is the sun. So before a person asks the sun to stir their thoughts, they first name where they stand: the ground, the air, the sky. That's the teaching in the frame. In Hindu prayer you don't ask from a small corner. You place yourself inside the whole of things, earth under your feet, the heavens over your head, and only then turn to Savitr. Many teachers read it that way: whatever you're carrying, an exam, a fight at home, gets said from the middle of three worlds. Om, then the three worlds, then the verse. So when someone says the Gayatri goes Om bhur bhuvah svah, tat savitur varenyam, they're describing how it's chanted, a living tradition of its own. The text and the recitation are both real. One begins at the verse, the other at the doorway in front of it.
screen: `NOT IN THE RIG VEDA'S TEXT.` · `OM, THEN THREE UTTERANCES.` · `EARTH, THE SPACE BETWEEN, THE SKY.` · `STAND IN ALL THREE WORLDS, THEN PRAY.`

segments.voice: Before the sit itself, stand at its threshold for three out-breaths, saying silently here, then between, then beyond, or bhur, bhuvah, svah if you pray. Then step through and rest, letting the breath come and go on its own. When the mind wanders, come back to the doorway, take the three breaths again, and step through once more.
The Gayatri in context. In recitation, the verse is framed by Om and three utterances: earth, the space between, and the sky beyond. The Rig Veda's verse itself begins at tat savitur. Today's word.
screen: `THE GAYATRI IN CONTEXT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: stand in all three worlds, then pray. Earth, the space between, the sky, and then the verse. See you tomorrow.

1266.title: The man who didn't know its mouth
1266.hook: King Janaka meets a man who claimed to know the Gayatri and is hauling loads like an elephant. what did he miss?
1266.carry: the gayatri's mouth is fire: it burns away wrong
1266.tomorrow: where does Krishna say he is the Gayatri?
1266.howItsDone: Hindus who keep sandhya offer water to the sun while saying the Gayatri, and many repeat it in japa as a cleansing; some teachers use the Upanishads' readings of it as a guide for meditation.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, stand in all three worlds, then pray: Om, then bhur, bhuvah, svah, earth, the space between, the sky, said before the verse.
screen: `OM, THEN THE THREE WORLDS.`

segments.voice: King Janaka of Videha, famous in the Upanishads for his wisdom, meets a man named Budila. Budila once claimed he knew the Gayatri inside out. And here he is, as the text puts it, become an elephant, hauling loads. So the king needles him: you called yourself a knower of the Gayatri, and look at you. What went wrong? That question closes a long passage on the verse in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. Today: what it means to really know the Gayatri.
screen: `A KING, AND A MAN WHO KNEW THE VERSE.` → `HAULING LOADS LIKE AN ELEPHANT.` → `WHAT WENT WRONG?`

segments.voice: Before the story, the Upanishad takes the verse apart. Its first line, eight syllables, is matched by earth, sky and heaven: bhumir, antariksham, dyauh, eight syllables too. The second by the three kinds of Vedic verse, rik, yajus and saman: the whole of sacred speech. The third by the three breaths, prana, apana and vyana: the whole of life. Worlds, words, breath. Then a fourth foot, the visible one beyond all dust, the sun that blazes. And the name: the Gayatri protects the gayas, the breaths, so it's called gayatri, the text says, offered as a meditation more than a dictionary entry. Budila, it seems, knew all of that. Then comes Janaka's question, and Budila's answer, in paraphrase: great king, I didn't know its mouth. Its mouth, the text says, is fire. Pile any amount of wood on a fire and it burns it all. In the same way, whoever knows this, whatever wrong they've done, burns it all away and comes out clean, pure, ageless, deathless. That's the teaching under the riddle. Knowing the verse's parts isn't knowing the verse. Its mouth is fire: the Gayatri is meant to burn something away in the one who says it. Hindu practice has long used the verse this way, to purify: offering water to the sun with it at sandhya, repeating it in japa. One way to hear Budila's answer: you can recite a prayer for years and still carry the same loads. The words have to be let in.
screen: `WORLDS, WORDS, BREATH.` · `A FOURTH FOOT: THE SUN THAT BLAZES.` · `ITS MOUTH IS FIRE.` · `THE WORDS HAVE TO BE LET IN.`

segments.voice: Before you begin, name one thing you'd like burned away: a grudge, a habit, a heaviness you keep carrying. Then, if you chant, say the Gayatri slowly, or hold its meaning, may our thoughts be stirred, line by line. Picture each line going in, not out, like wood fed into a fire. If you don't pray, simply name the weight, breathe in, out and through, and let a little of it go with each out-breath.
The Gayatri in context. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, its lines hold worlds, words and breath, and its mouth is fire. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: the Gayatri's mouth is fire, it burns away wrong. Know the words, and let them in. I'll be here tomorrow.

1267.title: Among meters, I am the Gayatri
1267.hook: in the Gita, Krishna names where he can be seen. among meters, he says, I am the Gayatri
1267.carry: vibhuti: god shows through the best of each thing
1267.tomorrow: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna
1267.howItsDone: Hindus who read the Bhagavad Gita meet its tenth chapter, where Krishna names his vibhutis, the things in which his glory can be seen, including, among meters, the Gayatri; it is one reason rivers, mountains and verses are honored as sacred.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri's mouth is fire: it burns away wrong. In the Brihadaranyaka, its lines hold worlds, words and breath.
screen: `ITS MOUTH IS FIRE.`

segments.voice: Out of all the mountains, which one? Out of all the rivers? In the tenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna how to recognize him in the world, and Krishna answers with a long list. Among bodies of water, the ocean. Among trees, the sacred fig. And in the middle, a line about poetry: among meters, I am the Gayatri. Today: the Gayatri in the Gita, and a look back at a week of placing one verse.
screen: `WHICH MOUNTAIN? WHICH RIVER?` → `KRISHNA ANSWERS WITH A LIST.` → `AMONG METERS, THE GAYATRI.`

segments.voice: In the tenth chapter Krishna describes his vibhutis, the ways his glory shows through the world, naming in each kind of thing the one where he can be seen. In verse thirty-five he says: among chants, I am the great Brihat-saman; among meters, the Gayatri; among months, Margashirsha; among seasons, spring. He names the meter; many readers hear the verse in it too. Then he sums up the list, in paraphrase: whatever is glorious, bright or mighty, know that it springs from a spark of my splendor. That's the teaching, plainly: vibhuti. In Hindu eyes God isn't only far away. He shows through the best of each kind of thing. It's part of why a river can be worshiped, a mountain walked around in prayer, a verse kept for a lifetime. For a life now, it means the moments that stop you, a song, a sunrise, someone's unexpected goodness, can be read as a glimpse. And it ends this week well. A king who wanted a cow became the seer of a prayer for light. Its god, Savitr, sends the day out and calls it home, so it's kept at dawn and dusk. Its meter gave it a name, and the law books call it the mother of a second birth. Om and three worlds open its door. Its mouth, an Upanishad says, is fire. And Krishna says: among meters, I am the Gayatri.
screen: `KRISHNA'S LIST OF WHERE HE SHOWS.` · `AMONG METERS, I AM THE GAYATRI.` · `A SPARK OF MY SPLENDOR.` · `ONE VERSE, SEEN FROM SIX SIDES.`

segments.voice: Let the week's pictures come back one at a time, without hurrying: a king setting down his weapons, the weaver rolling up her cloth, a verse whispered into an ear, the ground, the air and the sky, wood fed into a fire. Give each a breath or two and let it go. Then think of one thing this week that stopped you, a view, a voice, a kindness. If you pray, end with the Gayatri's meaning, may our thoughts be stirred, and name that moment as a glimpse of God.
